feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Integral of a Trigonometric Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice

question.name: Question 11
question.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}(x)-\int (x)(\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int {log}_{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{2}⁡x)(x)-\int (x)(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{2}⁡x-\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int \,\text{d}x \\  & =x{log}_{2}⁡x-\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =x{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}(x{log}_{2}⁡x-\frac{x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+D) \\  & =x{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2x{log}_{2}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}+\frac{2x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{x{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\frac{2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}+\frac{2x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}+C \\  & =\frac{x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{2D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{x}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+2)]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{e}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡e-2\operatorname{ln}⁡e+2)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}({ln}^{2}⁡1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2) \\  & =\frac{e}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}-\frac{2}{{ln}^{2}⁡2} \\  & =\frac{e-2}{{ln}^{2}⁡2}.\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 11
?

Evaluate ∫1e(log2⁡x)2dx.

a
 e−1ln⁡2
b
 2e+1ln2⁡2
c
 e+2ln2⁡2
d
 2e−1ln⁡2
e
 e−2ln2⁡2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define u=(log2⁡x)2⟹dudx=2log2⁡xxln⁡2dvdx=1⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫dx=x.

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫(log2⁡x)2dx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(log2⁡x)2(x)−∫(x)(2log2⁡xxln⁡2)dx=x(log2⁡x)2−2ln⁡2∫log2⁡xdx.

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate ∫log2⁡(x)dx. We take u=log2⁡x⟹dudx=1xln⁡2dvdx=1⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫dx=x.

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives ∫log2⁡xdx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(log2⁡x)(x)−∫(x)(1xln⁡2)dx=xlog2⁡x−1ln⁡2∫dx=xlog2⁡x−xln⁡2+D, where D is an integral constant.

So we have ∫(log2⁡x)2dx=x(log2⁡x)2−2ln⁡2(xlog2⁡x−xln⁡2+D)=x(log2⁡x)2−2xlog2⁡xln⁡2+2xln2⁡2+C=xln2⁡xln2⁡2−2xln⁡xln2⁡2+2xln2⁡2+C=xln2⁡2(ln2⁡x−2ln⁡x+2)+C, where C=−2Dln⁡2.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log2⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡2.

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral: ∫1e(log2⁡x)2dx=[xln2⁡2(ln2⁡x−2ln⁡x+2)]1e=eln2⁡2(ln2⁡e−2ln⁡e+2)−1ln2⁡2(ln2⁡1−2ln⁡1+2)=eln2⁡2−2ln2⁡2=e−2ln2⁡2.

last_observation.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({log}_{2}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}(x)-\int (x)(\frac{2{log}_{2}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2})\,\text{d}x \\  & =x{({log}_{2}⁡x)}^{2}-\frac{2}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}\int {log}_{2}⁡x\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate  $\int {log}_{2}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{2}⁡x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=1\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \,\text{d}x=x.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{2}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$

$$

Question 11
?

Evaluate ∫1e(log2⁡x)2dx.

a
 e−1ln⁡2
b
 2e+1ln2⁡2
c
 e+2ln2⁡2
d
 2e−1ln⁡2
e
 e−2ln2⁡2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define u=(log2⁡x)2⟹dudx=2log2⁡xxln⁡2dvdx=1⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫dx=x.

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫(log2⁡x)2dx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(log2⁡x)2(x)−∫(x)(2log2⁡xxln⁡2)dx=x(log2⁡x)2−2ln⁡2∫log2⁡xdx.

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate ∫log2⁡(x)dx. We take u=log2⁡x⟹dudx=1xln⁡2dvdx=1⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫dx=x.

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives ∫log2⁡xdx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(log2⁡x)(x)−∫(x)(1xln⁡2)dx=xlog2⁡x−1ln⁡2∫dx=xlog2⁡x−xln⁡2+D, where D is an integral constant.

So we have ∫(log2⁡x)2dx=x(log2⁡x)2−2ln⁡2(xlog2⁡x−xln⁡2+D)=x(log2⁡x)2−2xlog2⁡xln⁡2+2xln2⁡2+C=xln2⁡xln2⁡2−2xln⁡xln2⁡2+2xln2⁡2+C=xln2⁡2(ln2⁡x−2ln⁡x+2)+C, where C=−2Dln⁡2.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log2⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡2.

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral: ∫1e(log2⁡x)2dx=[xln2⁡2(ln2⁡x−2ln⁡x+2)]1e=eln2⁡2(ln2⁡e−2ln⁡e+2)−1ln2⁡2(ln2⁡1−2ln⁡1+2)=eln2⁡2−2ln2⁡2=e−2ln2⁡2.

question.name: Question 12
question.worked_solution:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))^{2} & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}{x+1}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=27(x+1)^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 27(x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x=9(x+1)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 27(x+1)^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}(9(x+1)^{3})-\int (9(x+1)^{3})(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}{x+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =9(x+1)^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-18\int (x+1)^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int (x+1)^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1) & \,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x+1}\,, \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=(x+1)^{2} & \,⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int (x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{3}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int (x+1)^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)(\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{3})(\frac{1}{x+1})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}{3}-\frac{1}{3}\int (x+1)^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{(x+1)^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}{3}-\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 27(x+1)^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))^{2}\,\text{d}x & =9(x+1)^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-18\int (x+1)^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =9(x+1)^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-18(\frac{(x+1)^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)}{3}-\frac{(x+1)^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =9(x+1)^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-6(x+1)^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+2(x+1)^{3}-18D \\  & =(x+1)^{3}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+2)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-18D.$

Finally, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{e-1}27(x+1)^{2}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))^{2}\text{d}x & ={[(x+1)^{3}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1))}^{2}-6\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+1)+2)]}_{0}^{e-1} \\  & =[{e}^{3}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡e)}^{2}-6\operatorname{ln}⁡e+2)]-[{1}^{3}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡1)}^{2}-6\operatorname{ln}⁡1+2)] \\  & =[{e}^{3}(9-6+2)]-2 \\  & =5{e}^{3}-2\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

question.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=4x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x=2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{3}⁡x)}^{2}(2{x}^{2})-\int (2{x}^{2})(\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int x{log}_{3}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int x{log}_{3}⁡(x)\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int x\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{log}_{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{3}⁡x)(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D) \\  & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{2{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}-\frac{2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{4D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$ 

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡e-2\operatorname{ln}⁡e+1)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2-2+1)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(0-0+1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives ∫4x(log3⁡x)2dx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(log3⁡x)2(2x2)−∫(2x2)(2log3⁡xxln⁡3)dx=2x2(log3⁡x)2−4ln⁡3∫xlog3⁡(x)dx.

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate ∫xlog3⁡(x)dx. We take

u=log3⁡(x)⟹dudx=1xln⁡3dvdx=x⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫xdx=x22.

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives ∫xlog3⁡xdx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(log3⁡x)(x22)−∫(x22)(1xln⁡3)dx=x2log3⁡x2−12ln⁡3∫xdx=x2log3⁡x2−x24ln⁡3+D, where D is a constant.

So, we get that the indefinite integral is ∫4x(log3⁡x)2dx=2x2(log3⁡x)2−4ln⁡3(x2log3⁡x2−x24ln⁡3+D)=2x2(log3⁡x)2−2x2log3⁡xln⁡3+x2ln2⁡3+C=2x2ln2⁡xln2⁡3−2x2ln⁡xln2⁡3+x2ln2⁡3+C=x2ln2⁡3(2ln2⁡x−2ln⁡x+1)+C, where C=−4Dln⁡3.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log3⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡3.

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral: ∫1e4x(log3⁡x)2dx=[x2ln2⁡3(2ln2⁡x−2ln⁡x+1)]1e=e2ln2⁡3(2ln2⁡e−2ln⁡e+1)−12ln2⁡3(2ln2⁡1−2ln⁡1+1)=e2ln2⁡3(2−2+1)−1ln2⁡3(0−0+1)=e2−1ln2⁡3.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
last_observation.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=4x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x=2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{3}⁡x)}^{2}(2{x}^{2})-\int (2{x}^{2})(\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int x{log}_{3}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int x{log}_{3}⁡(x)\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int x\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{log}_{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{3}⁡x)(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D) \\  & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{2{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}-\frac{2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{4D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$ 

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡e-2\operatorname{ln}⁡e+1)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2-2+1)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(0-0+1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Evaluate ∫1e4x(log3⁡x)2dx.

a
 e2−1ln2⁡3
b
 1−2eln2⁡3
c
 e2+2ln2⁡3
d
 2e2−1
e
 8e
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define u=(log3⁡x)2⟹dudx=2log3⁡xxln⁡3dvdx=4x⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫4xdx=2x2.

This gives ∫4x(log3⁡x)2dx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(log3⁡x)2(2x2)−∫(2x2)(2log3⁡xxln⁡3)dx=2x2(log3⁡x)2−4ln⁡3∫xlog3⁡(x)dx.

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate ∫xlog3⁡(x)dx. We take

u=log3⁡(x)⟹dudx=1xln⁡3dvdx=x⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫xdx=x22.

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives ∫xlog3⁡xdx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(log3⁡x)(x22)−∫(x22)(1xln⁡3)dx=x2log3⁡x2−12ln⁡3∫xdx=x2log3⁡x2−x24ln⁡3+D, where D is a constant.

So, we get that the indefinite integral is ∫4x(log3⁡x)2dx=2x2(log3⁡x)2−4ln⁡3(x2log3⁡x2−x24ln⁡3+D)=2x2(log3⁡x)2−2x2log3⁡xln⁡3+x2ln2⁡3+C=2x2ln2⁡xln2⁡3−2x2ln⁡xln2⁡3+x2ln2⁡3+C=x2ln2⁡3(2ln2⁡x−2ln⁡x+1)+C, where C=−4Dln⁡3.

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula log3⁡x=ln⁡xln⁡3.

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral: ∫1e4x(log3⁡x)2dx=[x2ln2⁡3(2ln2⁡x−2ln⁡x+1)]1e=e2ln2⁡3(2ln2⁡e−2ln⁡e+1)−12ln2⁡3(2ln2⁡1−2ln⁡1+1)=e2ln2⁡3(2−2+1)−1ln2⁡3(0−0+1)=e2−1ln2⁡3.
question.knowledge_point: Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice

solution.reasoning: Using log_3(x)=ln(x)/ln(3), an antiderivative is x^2(2(ln x)^2−2ln x+1)/(ln 3)^2. Evaluating from 1 to e gives (e^2−1)/(ln 3)^2, option a. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked example concerns a different integral.

feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{1}^{e}4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x.$
feedback.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u=({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=4x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x=2{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={({log}_{3}⁡x)}^{2}(2{x}^{2})-\int (2{x}^{2})(\frac{2{log}_{3}⁡x}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int x{log}_{3}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int x{log}_{3}⁡(x)\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u={log}_{3}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=x\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int x\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{log}_{3}⁡x\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({log}_{3}⁡x)(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})-\int (\frac{{x}^{2}}{2})(\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{1}{2\operatorname{ln}⁡3}\int x\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is a constant. 

So, we get that the indefinite integral is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{4}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}(\frac{{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{2}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+D) \\  & =2{x}^{2}({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}-\frac{2{x}^{2}{log}_{3}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}{ln}^{2}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}-\frac{2{x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-\frac{4D}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$ 

Note that in the above calculation we used the change of base formula ${log}_{3}⁡x=\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}.$

Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{1}^{e}4x({log}_{3}⁡x)^{2}\,\text{d}x & ={[\frac{{x}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡x-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)]}_{1}^{e} \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡e-2\operatorname{ln}⁡e+1)-\frac{{1}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2{ln}^{2}⁡1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡1+1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(2-2+1)-\frac{1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}(0-0+1) \\  & =\frac{{e}^{2}-1}{{ln}^{2}⁡3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}))(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{2}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}}{3}-\frac{16}{3}(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}}{3}-\frac{16{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{9}+\frac{32{x}^{3}}{27}-\frac{16D}{3} \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{3}}{27}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}-12\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}+8)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

Where, $C=-\frac{16D}{3}.$

Question 15
?

∫4x2(ln⁡x2)2dx=

a
x327(6(ln⁡x2)2+4ln⁡x2−1)+C
b
2x227(3(ln⁡x2)2−7ln⁡x2+5)+C
c
4x327(9(ln⁡x2)2−12ln⁡x2+8)+C
d
4x39(3(ln⁡x2)2+ln⁡x2+2)+C
e
2x29((ln⁡x2)2+ln⁡x2−4)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define u=(ln⁡x2)2⟹dudx=2ln⁡x2⋅1x2⋅2x=4ln⁡x2xdvdx=4x2⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫4x2dx=4x33.

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫4x2(ln⁡x2)2dx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(ln⁡x2)2(4x33)−∫(4x33)(4ln⁡x2x)dx=4x3(ln⁡x2)23−163∫x2ln⁡(x2)dx.

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate ∫x2ln⁡(x2)dx. We take u=ln⁡(x2)⟹dudx=2xdvdx=x2⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫x2dx=x33.

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives ∫x2ln⁡(x2)dx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(ln⁡(x2))(x33)−∫(x33)(2x)dx=x3ln⁡(x2)3−23∫x2dx=x3ln⁡(x2)3−2x39+D, where D is an integral constant.

So we have ∫4x2(ln⁡x2)2dx=4x3(ln⁡x2)23−163(x3ln⁡(x2)3−2x39+D)=4x3(ln⁡x2)23−16x3ln⁡(x2)9+32x327−16D3=4x327(9(ln⁡x2)2−12ln⁡x2+8)+C, Where, C=−16D3.

last_observation.name: Question 15
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice
last_observation.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x=\frac{4\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=4{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 4{x}^{2}\,\,\text{d}x=\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{2}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{4\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}}{3}-\frac{16}{3}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}))(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{2}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}}{3}-\frac{16}{3}(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}}{3}-\frac{16{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{9}+\frac{32{x}^{3}}{27}-\frac{16D}{3} \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{3}}{27}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}-12\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}+8)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

Where, $C=-\frac{16D}{3}.$

question.html:
Question 15
?

∫4x2(ln⁡x2)2dx=

a
x327(6(ln⁡x2)2+4ln⁡x2−1)+C
b
2x227(3(ln⁡x2)2−7ln⁡x2+5)+C
c
4x327(9(ln⁡x2)2−12ln⁡x2+8)+C
d
4x39(3(ln⁡x2)2+ln⁡x2+2)+C
e
2x29((ln⁡x2)2+ln⁡x2−4)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define u=(ln⁡x2)2⟹dudx=2ln⁡x2⋅1x2⋅2x=4ln⁡x2xdvdx=4x2⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫4x2dx=4x33.

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫4x2(ln⁡x2)2dx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(ln⁡x2)2(4x33)−∫(4x33)(4ln⁡x2x)dx=4x3(ln⁡x2)23−163∫x2ln⁡(x2)dx.

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate ∫x2ln⁡(x2)dx. We take u=ln⁡(x2)⟹dudx=2xdvdx=x2⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫x2dx=x33.

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives ∫x2ln⁡(x2)dx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(ln⁡(x2))(x33)−∫(x33)(2x)dx=x3ln⁡(x2)3−23∫x2dx=x3ln⁡(x2)3−2x39+D, where D is an integral constant.

So we have ∫4x2(ln⁡x2)2dx=4x3(ln⁡x2)23−163(x3ln⁡(x2)3−2x39+D)=4x3(ln⁡x2)23−16x3ln⁡(x2)9+32x327−16D3=4x327(9(ln⁡x2)2−12ln⁡x2+8)+C, Where, C=−16D3.

solution.reasoning: Let L=ln(x^2), so L'=2/x for x≠0. Differentiating option c gives (4x^2/27)[3(9L^2−12L+8)+2(18L−12)]=4x^2L^2, exactly the integrand. No Math Academy answer or grade for this question is captured; the supplied worked example concerns a different integral.

feedback.name: Question 15
feedback.problem: $\int 4{x}^{2}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\,\,\text{d}x=$
feedback.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\cdot 2x=\frac{4\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=4{x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int 4{x}^{2}\,\,\text{d}x=\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{2}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{4{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{4\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}}{3}-\frac{16}{3}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate $\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2}{x} \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}={x}^{2}\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x=\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int {x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}))(\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})-\int (\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})(\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2}{3}\int {x}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{9}+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 4{x}^{2}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}}{3}-\frac{16}{3}(\frac{{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{3}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{9}+D) \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{3}{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}}{3}-\frac{16{x}^{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2})}{9}+\frac{32{x}^{3}}{27}-\frac{16D}{3} \\  & =\frac{4{x}^{3}}{27}(9{(\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2})}^{2}-12\operatorname{ln}⁡{x}^{2}+8)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

Where, $C=-\frac{16D}{3}.$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get ∫4x2(ln⁡x2)2dx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(ln⁡x2)2(4x33)−∫(4x33)(4ln⁡x2x)dx=4x3(ln⁡x2)23−163∫x2ln⁡(x2)dx.

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate ∫x2ln⁡(x2)dx. We take u=ln⁡(x2)⟹dudx=2xdvdx=x2⟹v=∫dvdxdx=∫x2dx=x33.

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives ∫x2ln⁡(x2)dx=∫udvdxdx=uv−∫vdudxdx=(ln⁡(x2))(x33)−∫(x33)(2x)dx=x3ln⁡(x2)3−23∫x2dx=x3ln⁡(x2)3−2x39+D, where D is an integral constant.

So we have ∫4x2(ln⁡x2)2dx=4x3(ln⁡x2)23−163(x3ln⁡(x2)3−2x39+D)=4x3(ln⁡x2)23−16x3ln⁡(x2)9+32x327−16D3=4x327(9(ln⁡x2)2−12ln⁡x2+8)+C, Where, C=−16D3.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.worked_solution:
The range of $f(x)$ consists of all the outputs that have a corresponding $x$-input.

In a table, the range consists of all numbers that feature in the row corresponding to $h(x).$

Therefore, the range is the set $\{-5,-\frac{2}{5},0,1,\frac{3}{2},3,4,\frac{9}{2}\}.$

Question 1
?

What is the range of the function h defined by the following table?

x −5 −25 0 1 32 3 4 92
h(x) 92 4 3 32 1 0 −25 −5
a
{−5,−25,0,1,32,3,4,92}
b
(−∞,92]
c
[−5,92]
d
{−5,−2,0,1,2,3,9}
e
{−5,92}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The range of f(x) consists of all the outputs that have a corresponding x-input.

In a table, the range consists of all numbers that feature in the row corresponding to h(x).

Therefore, the range is the set {−5,−25,0,1,32,3,4,92}.

question.html:
Question 1
?

What is the range of the function h defined by the following table?

x −5 −25 0 1 32 3 4 92
h(x) 92 4 3 32 1 0 −25 −5
a
{−5,−25,0,1,32,3,4,92}
b
(−∞,92]
c
[−5,92]
d
{−5,−2,0,1,2,3,9}
e
{−5,92}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The range of f(x) consists of all the outputs that have a corresponding x-input.

In a table, the range consists of all numbers that feature in the row corresponding to h(x).

Therefore, the range is the set {−5,−25,0,1,32,3,4,92}.

question.html:
Question 1
?

What is the range of the function h defined by the following table?

x −5 −25 0 1 32 3 4 92
h(x) 92 4 3 32 1 0 −25 −5
a
{−5,−25,0,1,32,3,4,92}
b
(−∞,92]
c
[−5,92]
d
{−5,−2,0,1,2,3,9}
e
{−5,92}
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The range of f(x) consists of all the outputs that have a corresponding x-input.

In a table, the range consists of all numbers that feature in the row corresponding to h(x).

Therefore, the range is the set {−5,−25,0,1,32,3,4,92}.

question.html:
Question 2
?

What is the range of the function h defined by the following table?

x 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7
h(x) 12 32 52 12 32 52 −12 32
a
{−52,−32,−12,12,32,52}
b
{12,32,52}
c
{0,12,32,52}
d
{−12,52}
e
{−12,12,32,52}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The range of h(x) consists of all the outputs that have a corresponding x-input.

In a table, the range consists of all numbers that feature in the row corresponding to h(x).

Therefore, the range is the set {−12,12,32,52}.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
The range of $h(x)$ consists of all the outputs that have a corresponding $x$-input.

In a table, the range consists of all numbers that feature in the row corresponding to $h(x).$

Therefore, the range is the set $\{-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2},\frac{5}{2}\}.$

h(x) 12 32 52 12 32 52 −12 32
a
{−52,−32,−12,12,32,52}
b
{12,32,52}
c
{0,12,32,52}
d
{−12,52}
e
{−12,12,32,52}
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The range of h(x) consists of all the outputs that have a corresponding x-input.

In a table, the range consists of all numbers that feature in the row corresponding to h(x).

Therefore, the range is the set {−12,12,32,52}.

question.html:
Question 3
?

What is the range of the function h defined by the following table?

x 0 1 −2 3 −4 5 −6 7
h(x) −7 6 −5 4 −3 6 −1 0
a
{−7,0}
b
{−7,−5,−3,−1,0,2,4,6}
c
{−7,−5,−3,−1,0,4,6}
d
(−7,0)
e
[−7,6]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The range of h(x) consists of all the outputs that have a corresponding x-input.

In a table, the range consists of all numbers that feature in the row corresponding to h(x).

Therefore, the range is the set {−7,−5,−3,−1,0,4,6}.

The (population) linear correlation coefficient of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}
$$

where $\text{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance, and ${\sigma }_{x}$ and ${\sigma }_{y}$ are the standard deviations of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the covariance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(2-\frac{2}{3})(15-12)+(1-\frac{2}{3})(12-12)+(-1-\frac{2}{3})(9-12)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(\frac{4}{3})(3)+(\frac{1}{3})(0)+(-\frac{5}{3})(-3)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[4+0+5] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 9 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & ≈\frac{3}{1.247\cdot 2.449} \\  & ≈0.98\end{aligned}

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider the following data sets:

$$
x=\{7,\,2,\,12\},\,y=\{-1,\,9,\,7\}
$$

You're given that $\overset{―}{x}=7,$ $\overset{―}{y}=5,$ ${\sigma }_{x}≈4.082,$ and ${\sigma }_{y}≈4.320.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
The (population) linear correlation coefficient of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}
$$

where $\text{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance, and ${\sigma }_{x}$ and ${\sigma }_{y}$ are the standard deviations of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the covariance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(7-7)(-1-5)+(2-7)(9-5)+(12-7)(7-5)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(0)(-6)+(-5)(4)+(5)(2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[0-20+10] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-10) \\  & ≈-3.333\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & ≈\frac{(-3.333)}{4.082\cdot 4.320} \\  & ≈-0.19\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem:
The data sets $x$ and $y$ have the following properties:

$$
{S}_{xx}=41,\,{S}_{xy}=-39,\,{S}_{yy}=61
$$

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the definitions of ${S}_{xx},$ ${S}_{xy},$ and ${S}_{yy}$ for the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}:$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}
$$

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-39)}{\sqrt{41}\cdot \sqrt{61}} \\  & ≈-\frac{39}{6.403\,124\cdot 7.810\,250} \\  & ≈-0.78\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

questions.problem:
The data sets $x$ and $y$ have the following properties:

$$
{S}_{xx}=89,\,{S}_{xy}=-69,\,{S}_{yy}=426
$$

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the definitions of ${S}_{xx},$ ${S}_{xy},$ and ${S}_{yy}$ for the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}:$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}
$$

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-69)}{\sqrt{89}\cdot \sqrt{426}} \\  & ≈-\frac{69}{9.433\,981\cdot 20.639\,767} \\  & ≈-0.35\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem:
The data sets $x$ and $y$ have the following properties:

$$
{S}_{xx}=186,\,{S}_{xy}=2,\,{S}_{yy}=96
$$

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall the definitions of ${S}_{xx},$ ${S}_{xy},$ and ${S}_{yy}$ for the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}:$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}
$$

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{186}\cdot \sqrt{96}} \\  & ≈\frac{2}{13.638\,182\cdot 9.797\,959} \\  & ≈0.01\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem:
Consider the following data sets:

$$
x=\{13,\,4,\,10\},\,y=\{0,\,-3,\,9\}
$$

You are given that $\overset{―}{x}=9$ and $\overset{―}{y}=2.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

First, we compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(13-9)(0-2)+(4-9)(-3-2)+(10-9)(9-2) \\  & =(4)(-2)+(-5)(-5)+(1)(7) \\  & =-8+25+7 \\  & =24\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(13-9)^{2}+(4-9)^{2}+(10-9)^{2} \\  & =16+25+1 \\  & =42 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(0-2)^{2}+(-3-2)^{2}+(9-2)^{2} \\  & =4+25+49 \\  & =78\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{24}{\sqrt{42}\cdot \sqrt{78}} \\  & ≈\frac{24}{6.480\,741\cdot 8.831\,761} \\  & ≈0.42\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem:
Consider the following data sets:

$$
x=\{5,\,8,\,2\},\,y=\{-1,\,2,\,5\}
$$

You are given that $\overset{―}{x}=5$ and $\overset{―}{y}=2.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient.
questions.worked_solution:
The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

First, we compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(5-5)(-1-2)+(8-5)(2-2)+(2-5)(5-2) \\  & =(0)(-3)+(3)(0)+(-3)(3) \\  & =0+0-9 \\  & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(5-5)^{2}+(8-5)^{2}+(2-5)^{2} \\  & =0+9+9 \\  & =18 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(-1-2)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(5-2)^{2} \\  & =9+0+9 \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-9)}{\sqrt{18}\cdot \sqrt{18}} \\  & =-\frac{-9}{3\sqrt{2}\cdot 3\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-0.5\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
An ergonomist investigates $4$ factories. He wants to check the strength of the linear correlation between $x,$ the money spent by factory owners on safety training courses, and $y,$ the number of accidents per year in the factories. The data is shown below.

| **Money spent (hundreds of $$$)** | **$10$** | **$15$** | **$12$** | **$23$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Number of accidents** | $3$ | $6$ | $5$ | $2$ |

You are given that the means are $\overset{―}{x}=15$ and $\overset{―}{y}=4.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\rho ≈-0.45$

II. There is a strong negative correlation between $x$ and $y.$

III. There is a weak negative correlation between $x$ and $y.$

Hint: $|\rho |>0.7$ indicates a strong correlation, and $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7$ indicates a weak correlation.
questions.worked_solution:
The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

In addition, we have the following rule of thumb:

- if $|\rho |>0.7,$ the correlation is *strong*

- if $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7,$ the correlation is *weak*

- if $|\rho |<0.3,$ then the correlation is *negligible*

Let's now examine our statements in turn:

- Statement I is true. To calculate $\rho ,$ we first compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(10-15)(3-4)+(15-15)(6-4) \\  & +(12-15)(5-4)+(23-15)(2-4) \\  & =(-5)(-1)+(0)(2)+(-3)(1)+(8)(-2) \\  & =5+0-3-16 \\  & =-14\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(10-15)^{2}+(15-15)^{2}+(12-15)^{2}+(23-15)^{2} \\  & =25+0+9+64 \\  & =98 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(3-4)^{2}+(6-4)^{2}+(5-4)^{2}+(2-4)^{2} \\  & =1+4+1+4 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{-14}{\sqrt{98}\cdot \sqrt{10}} \\  & ≈-\frac{14}{9.899\,495\cdot 3.162\,278} \\  & ≈-0.45,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

- Statement II is false while statement III is true. Since $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7,$ the correlation is weak. Also, since $\rho $ is negative, the correlation is negative.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
Olivia plays soccer. She wants to check the strength of the linear correlation between the following variables:

- $x,$ the ages of Olivia's teammates, in years, and

- $y,$ their weights, in kilograms.

You are given that $\text{Cov}(x,y)=8,$ ${\sigma }_{x}=2,$ and ${\sigma }_{y}=5.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\rho =0.8$

II. There is a strong positive correlation between $x$ and $y.$

III. There is a weak positive correlation between $x$ and $y.$

*Hint: $|\rho |>0.7$ indicates a strong correlation, and $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7$ indicates a weak correlation.*
questions.worked_solution:
The (population) linear correlation coefficient for data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

In addition, we have the following rule of thumb:

- if $|\rho |>0.7,$ the correlation is *strong*

- if $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7,$ the correlation is *weak*

- if $|\rho |<0.3,$ then the correlation is *negligible*

Let's now examine our statements in turn:

- Statement I is true. Calculating the correlation coefficient, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{8}{2\cdot 5} \\  & =\frac{4}{5} \\  & =0.8.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Since $|\rho |>0.7,$ the correlation is strong. Also, since $\rho $ is positive, the correlation is positive.

Therefore, the correct answer is " I and II only."

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
A teacher of a group of $4$ students wants to check the strength of the linear correlation between $x,$ the number of hours the students had slept the night before an exam, and $y,$ the student's score in the exam. The data is shown below. 

| **Number of hours** | $2$ | $4$ | $6$ | $8$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Score ** | $56$ | $68$ | $81$ | $79$ |

You are given that the means are $\overset{―}{x}=5$ and $\overset{―}{y}=71.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\rho ≈0.81$

II. There is a strong positive correlation between $x$ and $y.$

III. There is a weak positive correlation between $x$ and $y.$

*Hint: $|\rho |>0.7$ indicates a strong correlation, and $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7$ indicates a weak correlation.*
questions.worked_solution:
The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

In addition, we have the following rule of thumb:

- if $|\rho |>0.7,$ the correlation is *strong*

- if $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7,$ the correlation is *weak*

- if $|\rho |<0.3,$ then the correlation is *negligible*

Let's now examine our statements in turn:

- Statement I is false. To calculate $\rho ,$ we first compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(2-5)(56-71)+(4-5)(68-71) \\  & +(6-5)(81-71)+(8-5)(79-71) \\  & =(-3)(-15)+(-1)(-3)+(1)(10)+(3)(8) \\  & =45+3+10+24 \\  & =82\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(2-5)^{2}+(4-5)^{2}+(6-5)^{2}+(8-5)^{2} \\  & =9+1+1+9 \\  & =20 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(56-71)^{2}+(68-71)^{2}+(81-71)^{2}+(79-71)^{2} \\  & =225+9+100+64 \\  & =398\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{82}{\sqrt{20}\cdot \sqrt{398}} \\  & ≈\frac{82}{4.472\,136\cdot 19.949\,937} \\  & ≈0.92,\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true, while statement III is false. Since $|\rho |>0.7,$ the correlation is strong. Also, since $\rho $ is positive, the correlation is positive.

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

$$

In addition, we have the following rule of thumb:

- if $|\rho |>0.7,$ the correlation is *strong*

- if $0.3\le |\rho |\le 0.7,$ the correlation is *weak*

- if $|\rho |<0.3,$ then the correlation is *negligible*

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing the Correlation Coefficient Using Covariance and Standard Deviations
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following data sets:

$$
x = \big\{ 6, \: 3, \: -1, \: 0 \big\},\qquad
y = \big\{ 5, \: 7, \: -2, \: 6 \big\}
$$

You're given that $\overline{x}=2,$ $\overline{y}=4,$ $\sigma_x \approx 2.739,$ and $\sigma_y \approx 3.536.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The (population) linear correlation coefficient of the data sets $x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}$ and $y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho(x,y) =  \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x \cdot \sigma_y}
$$

where $\textrm{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance, and $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_y$ are the standard deviations of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the covariance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(6-2)(5-4)+(3-2)(7-4)+(-1-2)(-2-4)+(0-2)(6-4)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(4)(1)+(1)(3)+(-3)(-6)+(-2)(2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[4+3+18-4] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 21 \\  & =5.25\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & ≈\frac{5.25}{2.739\cdot 3.536} \\  & ≈0.54\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing the Linear Correlation Coefficient Using the Expanded Formula
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the following data sets:

$$
x = \big\{ 13, \: 10, \: 9, \: 12 \big\},\qquad
y = \big\{ -1, \: 3, \: 2, \: 4 \big\}
$$

You are given that $\overline{x}=11$ and $\overline{y}=2.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The linear correlation coefficient $\rho$ of the data sets $x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}$ and $y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho(x,y) =  \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x \cdot \sigma_y} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}.
$$

First, we compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(13-11)(-1-2)+(10-11)(3-2) \\  & +(9-11)(2-2)+(12-11)(4-2) \\  & =(2)(-3)+(-1)(1)+(-2)(0)+(1)(2) \\  & =-6-1+0+2 \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(13-11)^{2}+(10-11)^{2}+(9-11)^{2}+(12-11)^{2} \\  & =4+1+4+1 \\  & =10 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(-1-2)^{2}+(3-2)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(4-2)^{2} \\  & =9+1+0+4 \\  & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-5)}{\sqrt{10}\cdot \sqrt{14}} \\  & ≈-\frac{5}{3.162\,278\cdot 3.741\,657} \\  & ≈-0.42\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

canonical_examples.problem:
A stall selling lemonade is set up at a special four-day summer festival. The stall owner wants to check the strength of the linear correlation between $x,$ the temperature at $12\,\textrm{p.m},$ and $y,$ the number of cups of lemonade sold that day. The data is shown below. 

| **Temperature at 
 $12$ p.m. ($^\circ \mathrm{C}$)** | **$26$** | **$30$** | **$22$** | **$18$** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Cups of Lemonade Sold** | $100$ | $118$ | $124$ | $86$ |

You are given that the means are $\overline{x}=24$ and $\overline{y}=107.$ Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\rho\approx 0.54$

II. There is a strong positive correlation between $x$ and $y.$

III. There is a weak positive correlation between $x$ and $y.$

*Hint: $|\rho| > 0.7$ indicates a strong correlation, and $0.3 \leq |\rho| \leq 0.7$ indicates a weak correlation.*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The linear correlation coefficient $\rho$ of the data sets $x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}$ and $y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho(x,y) =  \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x \cdot \sigma_y} = 
\dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}.
$$

In addition, we have the following rule of thumb:

- if $|\rho| \gt 0.7,$ the correlation is *strong*

- if $0.3\leq |\rho| \leq 0.7,$ the correlation is *weak*

- if $|\rho| \lt 0.3,$ then the correlation is *negligible*

Let's now examine our statements in turn:

- Statement I is true. To calculate $\rho,$ we first compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(26-24)(100-107)+(30-24)(118-107) \\  & +(22-24)(124-107)+(18-24)(86-107) \\  & =(2)(-7)+(6)(11)+(-2)(17)+(-6)(-21) \\  & =-14+66-34+126 \\  & =144\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(26-24)^{2}+(30-24)^{2}+(22-24)^{2}+(18-24)^{2} \\  & =4+36+4+36 \\  & =80 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(100-107)^{2}+(118-107)^{2}+(124-107)^{2}+(86-107)^{2} \\  & =49+121+289+441 \\  & =900\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{144}{\sqrt{80}\cdot \sqrt{900}} \\  & ≈\frac{144}{8.944\,272\cdot 30} \\  & ≈0.54,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Since $0.3\leq |\rho| \leq 0.7$ the correlation is weak. Also, since $\rho$ is positive, the correlation is positive.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

tutorials.name: Calculating the Correlation Coefficient
tutorials.problem:
To calculate $\rho,$ we use the following formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}},\end{aligned}
$$

where 

- $\textrm{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance between $x$ and $y,$ and

- $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_y$ are the standard deviations of $x$ and $y,$ respectively.

For example, consider data sets $x$ and $y$ such that 

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y)=-9, \qquad \sigma_x=6, \qquad \sigma_y=2.
$$

Substituting our numbers into the formula above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-9)}{(6)\cdot (2)} \\  & =\frac{(-9)}{12} \\  & =-0.75.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $|\rho| \gt 0.7,$ the correlation is strong. Also, since $\rho$ is negative, the correlation is negative.

Therefore, there is a strong negative correlation between $x$ and $y.$

tutorials.name: The Linear Correlation Coefficient in Sigma Notation
tutorials.problem:
Suppose we have data sets $x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}$ and $y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}$ of the same size.

Let's now introduce the following notation:

$$
S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2, 
\qquad S_{yy} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i-\overline{y})^2,
\qquad S_{xy} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y})
$$

Notice that $S_{xx}, S_{yy},$ and $S_{xy}$ are the sums of square deviations found in the formulas for the variance of $x,$ the variance of $y,$ and covariance of $x$ and $y,$ respectively. 

Using the previous definition, we can show that the correlation coefficient can be calculated as follows:

$$
\rho = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}\,.
$$

tutorials.name: Proving the Formula for Rho in Terms of Squared Deviations
tutorials.problem:
Let's derive the following result:

$$
\rho = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}
$$

We start with the definition of the correlation coefficient $\rho\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

We have

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) = \dfrac1n \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y}) = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{n}.
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{x} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{xx}}{n}} \\ {\sigma }_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{yy}}{n}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our definition for $\rho,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n})}{\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{xx}}{n}}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{S}_{yy}}{n}}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n})}{\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}{{n}^{2}}}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n})}{(\frac{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}{n})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\cancel{n}})}{(\frac{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}{\cancel{n}})} \\  & =\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The (population) linear correlation coefficient of the data sets $x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}$ and $y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho(x,y) =  \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x \cdot \sigma_y}
$$

where $\textrm{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance, and $\sigma_x$ and $\sigma_y$ are the standard deviations of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the covariance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(6-2)(5-4)+(3-2)(7-4)+(-1-2)(-2-4)+(0-2)(6-4)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[(4)(1)+(1)(3)+(-3)(-6)+(-2)(2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[4+3+18-4] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot 21 \\  & =5.25\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & ≈\frac{5.25}{2.739\cdot 3.536} \\  & ≈0.54\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Correlation Coefficient Using Covariance and Standard Deviations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The (population) linear correlation coefficient of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}
$$

where $\text{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance, and ${\sigma }_{x}$ and ${\sigma }_{y}$ are the standard deviations of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the covariance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(7-7)(-1-5)+(2-7)(9-5)+(12-7)(7-5)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(0)(-6)+(-5)(4)+(5)(2)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[0-20+10] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot (-10) \\  & ≈-3.333\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & ≈\frac{(-3.333)}{4.082\cdot 4.320} \\  & ≈-0.19\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

tutorial.name: The Linear Correlation Coefficient in Sigma Notation
tutorial.problem:
Suppose we have data sets $x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}$ and $y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}$ of the same size.

Let's now introduce the following notation:

$$
S_{xx} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})^2, 
\qquad S_{yy} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (y_i-\overline{y})^2,
\qquad S_{xy} = \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y})
$$

Notice that $S_{xx}, S_{yy},$ and $S_{xy}$ are the sums of square deviations found in the formulas for the variance of $x,$ the variance of $y,$ and covariance of $x$ and $y,$ respectively. 

Using the previous definition, we can show that the correlation coefficient can be calculated as follows:

$$
\rho = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}\,.
$$

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Correlation Coefficient Using Covariance and Standard Deviations
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The linear correlation coefficient $\rho$ of the data sets $x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}$ and $y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho(x,y) =  \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x \cdot \sigma_y} = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}.
$$

First, we compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(13-11)(-1-2)+(10-11)(3-2) \\  & +(9-11)(2-2)+(12-11)(4-2) \\  & =(2)(-3)+(-1)(1)+(-2)(0)+(1)(2) \\  & =-6-1+0+2 \\  & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(13-11)^{2}+(10-11)^{2}+(9-11)^{2}+(12-11)^{2} \\  & =4+1+4+1 \\  & =10 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(-1-2)^{2}+(3-2)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(4-2)^{2} \\  & =9+1+0+4 \\  & =14\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-5)}{\sqrt{10}\cdot \sqrt{14}} \\  & ≈-\frac{5}{3.162\,278\cdot 3.741\,657} \\  & ≈-0.42\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

observed_steps.worked_solution:

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-69)}{\sqrt{89}\cdot \sqrt{426}} \\  & ≈-\frac{69}{9.433\,981\cdot 20.639\,767} \\  & ≈-0.35\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

observed_steps.name: Example: Interpreting Linear Correlation Coefficients in Context
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Linear Correlation Coefficient Using the Expanded Formula
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The linear correlation coefficient $\rho$ of the data sets $x=\big\{ x_1,x_2, \ldots, x_n \big\}$ and $y=\big\{ y_1,y_2, \ldots, y_n \big\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho(x,y) =  \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}(x,y)}{\sigma_x \cdot \sigma_y} = 
\dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}.
$$

In addition, we have the following rule of thumb:

- if $|\rho| \gt 0.7,$ the correlation is *strong*

- if $0.3\leq |\rho| \leq 0.7,$ the correlation is *weak*

- if $|\rho| \lt 0.3,$ then the correlation is *negligible*

Let's now examine our statements in turn:

- Statement I is true. To calculate $\rho,$ we first compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(26-24)(100-107)+(30-24)(118-107) \\  & +(22-24)(124-107)+(18-24)(86-107) \\  & =(2)(-7)+(6)(11)+(-2)(17)+(-6)(-21) \\  & =-14+66-34+126 \\  & =144\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(26-24)^{2}+(30-24)^{2}+(22-24)^{2}+(18-24)^{2} \\  & =4+36+4+36 \\  & =80 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(100-107)^{2}+(118-107)^{2}+(124-107)^{2}+(86-107)^{2} \\  & =49+121+289+441 \\  & =900\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{144}{\sqrt{80}\cdot \sqrt{900}} \\  & ≈\frac{144}{8.944\,272\cdot 30} \\  & ≈0.54,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

- Statement II is false, while statement III is true. Since $0.3\leq |\rho| \leq 0.7$ the correlation is weak. Also, since $\rho$ is positive, the correlation is positive.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

tutorial.problem:
Let's derive the following result:

$$
\rho = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{\sqrt{S_{xx} \cdot S_{yy}}}
$$

We start with the definition of the correlation coefficient $\rho\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}\end{aligned}
$$

We have

$$
\textrm{Cov}(x,y) = \dfrac1n \sum\limits_{i=1}^n (x_i-\overline{x})(y_i-\overline{y}) = \dfrac{S_{xy}}{n}.
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\sigma }_{x} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{xx}}{n}} \\ {\sigma }_{y} & =\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{yy}}{n}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into our definition for $\rho,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n})}{\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{xx}}{n}}\cdot \sqrt{\frac{{S}_{yy}}{n}}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n})}{\sqrt{\frac{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}{{n}^{2}}}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{n})}{(\frac{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}{n})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\cancel{n}})}{(\frac{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}{\cancel{n}})} \\  & =\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
Consider the following data sets:

$$
x=\{2,\,1,\,-1\},\,y=\{15,\,12,\,9\}
$$

You're given that $\overset{―}{x}=\frac{2}{3},$ $\overset{―}{y}=12,$ ${\sigma }_{x}≈1.247,$ and ${\sigma }_{y}≈2.449.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
The (population) linear correlation coefficient of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}
$$

where $\text{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance, and ${\sigma }_{x}$ and ${\sigma }_{y}$ are the standard deviations of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the covariance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(2-\frac{2}{3})(15-12)+(1-\frac{2}{3})(12-12)+(-1-\frac{2}{3})(9-12)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(\frac{4}{3})(3)+(\frac{1}{3})(0)+(-\frac{5}{3})(-3)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[4+0+5] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 9 \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & ≈\frac{3}{1.247\cdot 2.449} \\  & ≈0.98\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

ρ(x,y)=Cov(x,y)σx⋅σy.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Consider the following data sets:

$$
x=\{23,\,21,\,25\},\,y=\{10,\,8,\,9\}
$$

You're given that $\overset{―}{x}=23,$ $\overset{―}{y}=9,$ ${\sigma }_{x}≈1.633,$ and ${\sigma }_{y}≈0.816.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
The (population) linear correlation coefficient of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}
$$

where $\text{Cov}(x,y)$ is the covariance, and ${\sigma }_{x}$ and ${\sigma }_{y}$ are the standard deviations of the data sets.

First, we need to compute the covariance:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}(x,y) & =\frac{1}{n}{\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(23-23)(10-9)+(21-23)(8-9)+(25-23)(9-9)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}[(0)(1)+(-2)(-1)+(2)(0)] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\cdot 2 \\  & ≈0.667\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}} \\  & ≈\frac{0.667}{1.633\cdot 0.816} \\  & ≈0.50\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.name: Question 6
question.problem:
The data sets $x$ and $y$ have the following properties:

$$
{S}_{xx}=41,\,{S}_{xy}=-39,\,{S}_{yy}=61
$$

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Recall the definitions of ${S}_{xx},$ ${S}_{xy},$ and ${S}_{yy}$ for the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}:$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}
$$

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-39)}{\sqrt{41}\cdot \sqrt{61}} \\  & ≈-\frac{39}{6.403\,124\cdot 7.810\,250} \\  & ≈-0.78\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.html:
Question 6
?

The data sets x and y have the following properties:

Sxx=41,Sxy=−39,Syy=61

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

a
ρ≈−0.57
b
ρ≈0.69
c
ρ≈−0.69
d
ρ≈0.78
e
ρ≈−0.78
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the definitions of Sxx, Sxy, and Syy for the data sets x={x1,x2,…,xn} and y={y1,y2,…,yn}:

Sxx=∑i=1n(xi−x―)2,Sxy=∑i=1n(xi−x―)(yi−y―),Syy=∑i=1n(yi−y―)2

The linear correlation coefficient ρ of the data sets x and y is given by

ρ(x,y)=Cov(x,y)σx⋅σy=SxySxx⋅Syy.

Using the formula, we get

ρ(x,y)=(−39)41⋅61≈−396.403124⋅7.810250≈−0.78

rounded to 2 decimal places.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem:
The data sets $x$ and $y$ have the following properties:

$$
{S}_{xx}=41,\,{S}_{xy}=-39,\,{S}_{yy}=61
$$

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall the definitions of ${S}_{xx},$ ${S}_{xy},$ and ${S}_{yy}$ for the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}:$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}
$$

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-39)}{\sqrt{41}\cdot \sqrt{61}} \\  & ≈-\frac{39}{6.403\,124\cdot 7.810\,250} \\  & ≈-0.78\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.problem:
The data sets $x$ and $y$ have the following properties:

$$
{S}_{xx}=89,\,{S}_{xy}=-69,\,{S}_{yy}=426
$$

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Recall the definitions of ${S}_{xx},$ ${S}_{xy},$ and ${S}_{yy}$ for the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}:$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}
$$

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-69)}{\sqrt{89}\cdot \sqrt{426}} \\  & ≈-\frac{69}{9.433\,981\cdot 20.639\,767} \\  & ≈-0.35\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Linear Correlation Coefficient Using the Expanded Formula
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall the definitions of ${S}_{xx},$ ${S}_{xy},$ and ${S}_{yy}$ for the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}:$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}
$$

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-69)}{\sqrt{89}\cdot \sqrt{426}} \\  & ≈-\frac{69}{9.433\,981\cdot 20.639\,767} \\  & ≈-0.35\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.problem:
The data sets $x$ and $y$ have the following properties:

$$
{S}_{xx}=186,\,{S}_{xy}=2,\,{S}_{yy}=96
$$

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Recall the definitions of ${S}_{xx},$ ${S}_{xy},$ and ${S}_{yy}$ for the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}:$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}
$$

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{186}\cdot \sqrt{96}} \\  & ≈\frac{2}{13.638\,182\cdot 9.797\,959} \\  & ≈0.01\end{aligned}

question.html:
Question 8
?

The data sets x and y have the following properties:

Sxx=186,Sxy=2,Syy=96

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

a
ρ≈0.01
b
ρ≈0.07
c
ρ≈0.21
d
ρ≈0.15
e
ρ≈0.03
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the definitions of Sxx, Sxy, and Syy for the data sets x={x1,x2,…,xn} and y={y1,y2,…,yn}:

Sxx=∑i=1n(xi−x―)2,Sxy=∑i=1n(xi−x―)(yi−y―),Syy=∑i=1n(yi−y―)2

The linear correlation coefficient ρ of the data sets x and y is given by

ρ(x,y)=Cov(x,y)σx⋅σy=SxySxx⋅Syy.

Using the formula, we get

ρ(x,y)=2186⋅96≈213.638182⋅9.797959≈0.01

rounded to 2 decimal places.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing the Linear Correlation Coefficient Using the Expanded Formula
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall the definitions of ${S}_{xx},$ ${S}_{xy},$ and ${S}_{yy}$ for the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}:$

$$
{S}_{xx}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2},\,{S}_{xy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}),\,{S}_{yy}={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2}
$$

The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x$ and $y$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

Using the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{2}{\sqrt{186}\cdot \sqrt{96}} \\  & ≈\frac{2}{13.638\,182\cdot 9.797\,959} \\  & ≈0.01\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

Question 8

The data sets x and y have the following properties:

Sxx=186,Sxy=2,Syy=96

Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

a
ρ≈0.01
b
ρ≈0.07
c
ρ≈0.21
d
ρ≈0.15
e
ρ≈0.03
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall the definitions of Sxx, Sxy, and Syy for the data sets x={x1,x2,…,xn} and y={y1,y2,…,yn}:

Sxx=∑i=1n(xi−x―)2,Sxy=∑i=1n(xi−x―)(yi−y―),Syy=∑i=1n(yi−y―)2

The linear correlation coefficient ρ of the data sets x and y is given by

ρ(x,y)=Cov(x,y)σx⋅σy=SxySxx⋅Syy.

Using the formula, we get

ρ(x,y)=2186⋅96≈213.638182⋅9.797959≈0.01

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
Consider the following data sets:

$$
x=\{13,\,4,\,10\},\,y=\{0,\,-3,\,9\}
$$

You are given that $\overset{―}{x}=9$ and $\overset{―}{y}=2.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

First, we compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(13-9)(0-2)+(4-9)(-3-2)+(10-9)(9-2) \\  & =(4)(-2)+(-5)(-5)+(1)(7) \\  & =-8+25+7 \\  & =24\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(13-9)^{2}+(4-9)^{2}+(10-9)^{2} \\  & =16+25+1 \\  & =42 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(0-2)^{2}+(-3-2)^{2}+(9-2)^{2} \\  & =4+25+49 \\  & =78\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{24}{\sqrt{42}\cdot \sqrt{78}} \\  & ≈\frac{24}{6.480\,741\cdot 8.831\,761} \\  & ≈0.42\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.html:
Question 9
?

Consider the following data sets: x={13,4,10},y={0,−3,9} You are given that x―=9 and y―=2. Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

a
ρ≈0.42
b
ρ≈0.46
c
ρ≈0.51
d
ρ≈−0.53
e
ρ≈−0.44
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The linear correlation coefficient ρ of the data sets x={x1,x2,…,xn} and y={y1,y2,…,yn} is given by

ρ(x,y)=Cov(x,y)σx⋅σy=SxySxx⋅Syy.

First, we compute the sum in the numerator:

Sxy=∑i=1n(xi−x―)(yi−y―)=(13−9)(0−2)+(4−9)(−3−2)+(10−9)(9−2)=(4)(−2)+(−5)(−5)+(1)(7)=−8+25+7=24

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

Sxx=∑i=1n(xi−x―)2=(13−9)2+(4−9)2+(10−9)2=16+25+1=42Syy=∑i=1n(yi−y―)2=(0−2)2+(−3−2)2+(9−2)2=4+25+49=78

Finally, we use the formula:

ρ(x,y)=2442⋅78≈246.480741⋅8.831761≈0.42

rounded to 2 decimal places.

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.problem:
Consider the following data sets:

$$
x=\{13,\,4,\,10\},\,y=\{0,\,-3,\,9\}
$$

You are given that $\overset{―}{x}=9$ and $\overset{―}{y}=2.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient. Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
feedback.worked_solution:
The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

First, we compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(13-9)(0-2)+(4-9)(-3-2)+(10-9)(9-2) \\  & =(4)(-2)+(-5)(-5)+(1)(7) \\  & =-8+25+7 \\  & =24\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(13-9)^{2}+(4-9)^{2}+(10-9)^{2} \\  & =16+25+1 \\  & =42 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(0-2)^{2}+(-3-2)^{2}+(9-2)^{2} \\  & =4+25+49 \\  & =78\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{24}{\sqrt{42}\cdot \sqrt{78}} \\  & ≈\frac{24}{6.480\,741\cdot 8.831\,761} \\  & ≈0.42\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.name: Question 10
question.problem:
Consider the following data sets:

$$
x=\{5,\,8,\,2\},\,y=\{-1,\,2,\,5\}
$$

You are given that $\overset{―}{x}=5$ and $\overset{―}{y}=2.$ Calculate the corresponding linear correlation coefficient.
question.worked_solution:
The linear correlation coefficient $\rho $ of the data sets $x=\{{x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}\}$ and $y=\{{y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n}\}$ is given by 

$$
\rho (x,y)=\frac{\text{Cov}(x,y)}{{\sigma }_{x}\cdot {\sigma }_{y}}=\frac{{S}_{xy}}{\sqrt{{S}_{xx}\cdot {S}_{yy}}}.
$$

First, we compute the sum in the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y}) \\  & =(5-5)(-1-2)+(8-5)(2-2)+(2-5)(5-2) \\  & =(0)(-3)+(3)(0)+(-3)(3) \\  & =0+0-9 \\  & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

Second, we compute the sums in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{xx} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({x}_{i}-\overset{―}{x})^{2} \\  & =(5-5)^{2}+(8-5)^{2}+(2-5)^{2} \\  & =0+9+9 \\  & =18 \\ {S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & =(-1-2)^{2}+(2-2)^{2}+(5-2)^{2} \\  & =9+0+9 \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we use the formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho (x,y) & =\frac{(-9)}{\sqrt{18}\cdot \sqrt{18}} \\  & =-\frac{-9}{3\sqrt{2}\cdot 3\sqrt{2}} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =-0.5\end{aligned}
$$
