questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14227047/assets/720713e7e1dbfbc9ce3ebb486e8744327c633745d00df7dc862d794eefe57bbc.png)

What is the least distance between the curve $y=\sqrt{x}$ and the point $(4,0)?$
questions.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(4,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-0)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{x})^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+16+x \\  & ={x}^{2}-7x+16.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-7 & =0 \\ 2x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{7}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{7}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(\frac{7}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(\frac{7}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-7(\frac{7}{2})+16} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{15}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Find the $y$-coordinate of the point on the curve $y={x}^{2}-2x$ that is closest to the point $(1,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(1,4)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{y}^{2}-8y+16 \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}-8y+17\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y={x}^{2}-2x.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(y) & =y+{y}^{2}-8y+17 \\  & ={y}^{2}-7y+17.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(y)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(y)=2y-7 & =0 \\ 2y & =7 \\ y & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(y)=2>0.$ Therefore, $y=\frac{7}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) is minimized when $y=\frac{7}{2}.$

{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,1)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1})^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & =2{x}^{2}-4x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=4x-4 & =0 \\ 4x & =4 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=4>0,$ so $x=1$ gives a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=1$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(1)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(1)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(1)^{2}-4(1)+5} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,2)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{|x-1|}+2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{(\sqrt{|x-1|}+2-2)}^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+|x-1|.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\ge 1,$ we have $|x-1|=x-1,$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-3 & =0 \\ 2x & =3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-3(\frac{3}{2})+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}-\frac{9}{2}+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let us consider the squared distance S between (4,0) and a general point P(x,y): S=(x−4)2+(y−0)2

We require that the point P lies on the curve y=x. Substituting this into the above gives S=(x−4)2+(y−0)2=(x−4)2+(x)2=x2−8x+16+x=x2−7x+16.

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of S(x) and equate it to zero. This gives the following: S′(x)=2x−7=02x=7x=72

We can see that S″(x)=2>0. Therefore, x=72 is a minimum of S.

Since S gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance d between the two points when x=72 is given by

d=S(72).

Computing this quantity, we get

d=S(72)=(72)2−7(72)+16=154=152.

Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(1,4)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{y}^{2}-8y+16 \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}-8y+17\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y={x}^{2}-2x.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(y) & =y+{y}^{2}-8y+17 \\  & ={y}^{2}-7y+17.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(y)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(y)=2y-7 & =0 \\ 2y & =7 \\ y & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(y)=2>0.$ Therefore, $y=\frac{7}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) is minimized when $y=\frac{7}{2}.$

Find the y-coordinate of the point on the curve y=x2−2x that is closest to the point (1,4).

a
y=194

c
y=72

y=172

Correct
EXPLANATION

Let us consider the squared distance S between (1,4) and a general point P(x,y):

S=(x−1)2+(y−4)2=x2−2x+1+y2−8y+16=x2−2x+y2−8y+17

We require that the point P lies on the curve y=x2−2x. Substituting this into the above gives

S(y)=y+y2−8y+17=y2−7y+17.

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of S(y) and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

S′(y)=2y−7=02y=7y=72

We can see that S″(y)=2>0. Therefore, y=72 is a minimum of S.

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) is minimized when y=72.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,1)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1})^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & =2{x}^{2}-4x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=4x-4 & =0 \\ 4x & =4 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=4>0,$ so $x=1$ gives a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=1$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(1)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(1)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(1)^{2}-4(1)+5} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,2)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{|x-1|}+2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{(\sqrt{|x-1|}+2-2)}^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+|x-1|.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\ge 1,$ we have $|x-1|=x-1,$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-3 & =0 \\ 2x & =3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-3(\frac{3}{2})+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}-\frac{9}{2}+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(4,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-0)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{x})^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+16+x \\  & ={x}^{2}-7x+16.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-7 & =0 \\ 2x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{7}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{7}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(\frac{7}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(\frac{7}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-7(\frac{7}{2})+16} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{15}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

What is the least distance between the curve y=x and the point (4,0)?

a
154
b
152
c
144
d
32
e
154
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let us consider the squared distance S between (4,0) and a general point P(x,y): S=(x−4)2+(y−0)2

We require that the point P lies on the curve y=x. Substituting this into the above gives S=(x−4)2+(y−0)2=(x−4)2+(x)2=x2−8x+16+x=x2−7x+16.

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of S(x) and equate it to zero. This gives the following: S′(x)=2x−7=02x=7x=72

We can see that S″(x)=2>0. Therefore, x=72 is a minimum of S.

Since S gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance d between the two points when x=72 is given by

d=S(72).

Computing this quantity, we get

d=S(72)=(72)2−7(72)+16=154=152.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(4,0)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-0)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{x}.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-4)^{2}+(y-0)^{2} \\  & =(x-4)^{2}+(\sqrt{x})^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-8x+16+x \\  & ={x}^{2}-7x+16.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-7 & =0 \\ 2x & =7 \\ x & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{7}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{7}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(\frac{7}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(\frac{7}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{7}{2})}^{2}-7(\frac{7}{2})+16} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{15}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{15}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: Find the $y$-coordinate of the point on the curve $y={x}^{2}-2x$ that is closest to the point $(1,4).$
question.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(1,4)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-1)^{2}+(y-4)^{2} \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+1+{y}^{2}-8y+16 \\  & ={x}^{2}-2x+{y}^{2}-8y+17\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y={x}^{2}-2x.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(y) & =y+{y}^{2}-8y+17 \\  & ={y}^{2}-7y+17.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(y)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(y)=2y-7 & =0 \\ 2y & =7 \\ y & =\frac{7}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(y)=2>0.$ Therefore, $y=\frac{7}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

So, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) is minimized when $y=\frac{7}{2}.$

Let us consider the squared distance S between (1,4) and a general point P(x,y):

S=(x−1)2+(y−4)2=x2−2x+1+y2−8y+16=x2−2x+y2−8y+17

We require that the point P lies on the curve y=x2−2x. Substituting this into the above gives

S(y)=y+y2−8y+17=y2−7y+17.

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of S(y) and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

S′(y)=2y−7=02y=7y=72

Find the least distance $d$ between the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1$ and the point $(2,1).$ Do not round the answer.

$d=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,1)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1})^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & =2{x}^{2}-4x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=4x-4 & =0 \\ 4x & =4 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=4>0,$ so $x=1$ gives a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=1$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(1)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(1)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(1)^{2}-4(1)+5} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$d=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,1)$ and a general point $P(x,y)$:

$$
S=(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S(x) & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1}+1-1)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+(\sqrt{{x}^{2}+1})^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+{x}^{2}+1 \\  & =2{x}^{2}-4x+5.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=4x-4 & =0 \\ 4x & =4 \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=4>0,$ so $x=1$ gives a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=1$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S(1)}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S(1)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(1)^{2}-4(1)+5} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.worked_solution:
Let us consider the *squared* distance $S$ between $(2,2)$ and a general point $P(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We require that the point $P$ lies on the curve $y=\sqrt{|x-1|}+2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+(y-2)^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+{(\sqrt{|x-1|}+2-2)}^{2} \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+|x-1|.\end{aligned}
$$

For $x\ge 1,$ we have $|x-1|=x-1,$ so

$$
\begin{aligned}S & =(x-2)^{2}+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-4x+4+x-1 \\  & ={x}^{2}-3x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

To find the minimum distance, we take the first derivative of $S(x)$ and equate it to zero. This gives the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(x)=2x-3 & =0 \\ 2x & =3 \\ x & =\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(x)=2>0.$ Therefore, $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is a minimum of $S.$

Since $S$ gives the squared distance between the two points, the actual distance $d$ between the two points when $x=\frac{3}{2}$ is given by

$$
d=\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})}.
$$

Computing this quantity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}d & =\sqrt{S\,(\frac{3}{2})} \\  & =\sqrt{{(\frac{3}{2})}^{2}-3(\frac{3}{2})+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{9}{4}-\frac{9}{2}+3} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{3}{4}} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Either the positive or negative of the expression inside the absolute value must be equal to the right-hand side of the equation.

So, we set up the two corresponding equations and solve them independently:

- If $|6x+1|=6x+1,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|6x+1| & =7 \\ 6x+1 & =7 \\ 6x & =6 \\ \frac{6x}{6} & =\frac{6}{6} \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|6x+1|=-(6x+1),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|6x+1| & =7 \\ -(6x+1) & =7 \\ -6x-1 & =7 \\ -6x & =8 \\ \frac{-6x}{-6} & =\frac{8}{-6} \\ x & =-\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-\frac{4}{3}$ and $x=1.$

questions.worked_solution:
We distribute both terms of the binomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(q+1)({q}^{2}+7q+2) & = \\ q({q}^{2}+7q+2)+1({q}^{2}+7q+2) & = \\ {q}^{3}+7{q}^{2}+2q+{q}^{2}+7q+2 & = \\ {q}^{3}+8{q}^{2}+9q+2\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve the remaining equation using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}21-3k & =4k \\ 21-3k+3k & =4k+3k \\ 21 & =7k \\ \frac{21}{7} & =\frac{7k}{7} \\ 3 & =\frac{\cancel{7}k}{\cancel{7}} \\ 3 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1

If |6x+1|=7, then x=

a
 −34 or 1
b
 −1 or 43
c
 −43 or −1
d
 −43 or 1
e
 −1 or 34

decision.exposure_note: KP association unavailable; use the base accuracy without pooling unknown skills

solution.reasoning: The absolute-value equation gives 6x+1=7 or 6x+1=-7, so x=1 or x=-4/3. This matches option d. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.worked_solution:
Either the positive or negative of the expression inside the absolute value must be equal to the right-hand side of the equation.

So, we set up the two corresponding equations and solve them independently:

- If $|6x+1|=6x+1,$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|6x+1| & =7 \\ 6x+1 & =7 \\ 6x & =6 \\ \frac{6x}{6} & =\frac{6}{6} \\ x & =1\end{aligned}
$$

- If $|6x+1|=-(6x+1),$ we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|6x+1| & =7 \\ -(6x+1) & =7 \\ -6x-1 & =7 \\ -6x & =8 \\ \frac{-6x}{-6} & =\frac{8}{-6} \\ x & =-\frac{4}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solutions are $x=-\frac{4}{3}$ and $x=1.$

question.html:
Question 2

Which of the following is equivalent to (q+1)(q2+7q+2)?

a
 q3+10q2+12q+2
b
 q3+8q2+9q+2
c
 q3+4q2+7q+2
d
 q3+4q2+3q+2
e
 q3+2q2+q+2

decision.exposure_note: KP association unavailable; use the base accuracy without pooling unknown skills

solution.reasoning: Distributing gives q^3+7q^2+2q+q^2+7q+2=q^3+8q^2+9q+2, matching option b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to $(q+1)({q}^{2}+7q+2)?$
feedback.worked_solution:
We distribute both terms of the binomial in the first set of parentheses to the trinomial in the second set of parentheses. Then, we simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}(q+1)({q}^{2}+7q+2) & = \\ q({q}^{2}+7q+2)+1({q}^{2}+7q+2) & = \\ {q}^{3}+7{q}^{2}+2q+{q}^{2}+7q+2 & = \\ {q}^{3}+8{q}^{2}+9q+2\end{aligned}
$$

solution.reasoning: Since 8x^3y^6=(2xy^2)^3, its real cube root is 2xy^2, matching option b. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.worked_solution:
We write the term under the radical as a perfect cube, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt[3]{8{x}^{3}{y}^{6}} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{2x{y}^{2}\cdot 2x{y}^{2}\cdot 2x{y}^{2}} & = \\ \sqrt[3]{{(2x{y}^{2})}^{3}} & = \\ 2x{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}{s}^{2}-\frac{1}{9} & = \\ {s}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2} & = \\ (s-\frac{1}{3})(s+\frac{1}{3})\end{aligned}

feedback.problem: If $k=\frac{21-3k}{4},$ then $k=${{field-1}}.
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we clear the rational expression by multiplying the equation through by $4$:

$$
\begin{aligned}k & =\frac{21-3k}{4} \\ \frac{21-3k}{4} & =k \\ 4(\frac{21-3k}{4}) & =4\cdot k \\ \cancel{4}(\frac{21-3k}{\cancel{4}}) & =4k \\ 21-3k & =4k\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we solve the remaining equation using the addition and multiplication principles:

$$
\begin{aligned}21-3k & =4k \\ 21-3k+3k & =4k+3k \\ 21 & =7k \\ \frac{21}{7} & =\frac{7k}{7} \\ 3 & =\frac{\cancel{7}k}{\cancel{7}} \\ 3 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $k=3.$

solution.reasoning: Let last year's attendance be T. This year's attendance is 1.2T, and art exhibit attendance is 0.9(1.2T)=1.08T, or 108% of last year's total. This matches option a. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.problem: Museum attendance increased to $120%$ of last year’s total. Of those visitors, $90%$ also attended the art exhibit. What percentage of last year’s total attended the art exhibit?
feedback.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the number of visitors last year.

We're told that attendance increased to $120%$ of last year’s total. Thus, the new number of visitors is $1.2x.$

We are also told that of those visitors, $90%$ attended the art exhibit. So, the number of visitors who attended the art exhibit is

$$
0.9(1.2x)=1.08x.
$$

The expression $1.08x$ represents $108%$ of $x.$ Therefore, $108%$ of last year’s total attended the art exhibit.

solution.reasoning: Use (4·3)^7=4^7·3^7, then combine powers of 4: 4^8·4^7·3^7=4^15·3^7. This matches option e. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated key.

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we rewrite the second factor using the power of product rule:

$$
{4}^{8}\cdot {(4\cdot 3)}^{7}={4}^{8}\cdot {4}^{7}\cdot {3}^{7}
$$

Finally, we apply the product rule for exponents, and simplify:

$$
{4}^{8}\cdot {4}^{7}\cdot {3}^{7}={4}^{8+7}\cdot {3}^{7}={4}^{15}\cdot {3}^{7}
$$

Which of the following values of $x$ satisfy the inequality $\frac{x}{5}>2\,?$

I. $x=30$

II. $x=15$

III. $x=10$
feedback.worked_solution:
We substitute each value into the given inequality and check to see if the resulting statement is true or false.

- We substitute the value $x=30$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{5} & >2 \\ \frac{30}{5} & >2 \\ 6 & >2\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $x=30$ into the inequality leads to a **true** statement. 

Therefore, $x=30$ **satisfies** this inequality.

- We substitute the value $x=15$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{5} & >2 \\ \frac{15}{5} & >2 \\ 3 & >2\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $x=15$ into the inequality leads to a **true** statement. 

Therefore, $x=15$ **satisfies** this inequality.

- We substitute the value $x=10$ into the given inequality. We get:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{5} & >2 \\ \frac{10}{5} & >2 \\ 2 & >2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

So, substituting $x=10$ into the inequality leads to a **false** statement. 

Therefore, $x=10$ **does not satisfy** this inequality.

solution.reasoning: Dividing by 81 gives a^2=16/81. Taking both square roots yields a=±4/9. The value 0 fails the original equation. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its stated answer.

feedback.worked_solution:
First, we isolate the ${a}^{2}$ on one side of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}81{a}^{2} & =16 \\ {a}^{2} & =\frac{16}{81}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we take the square root of both sides of the equation and solve the resulting absolute value equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{a}^{2}} & =\sqrt{\frac{16}{81}} \\ |a| & =\frac{\sqrt{16}}{\sqrt{81}} \\ |a| & =\frac{4}{9} \\ a & =\pm \frac{4}{9}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Given that $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=-3,$ $\text{SD}[X]=3,$ and $\text{SD}[Y]=2$, find the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: The variances of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ are $0.09$ and $0.16$, respectively. Given that $\text{Cov}(X,Y)=-0.03,$ find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{0.09}=0.3, \\ \text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[Y]}=\sqrt{0.16}=0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[X]} \\  & =\frac{-0.03}{0.3\cdot 0.4} \\  & =-0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=15,$ $\text{SD}[X]=10,$ and $\text{SD}[Y]=5$, find the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & =\frac{15}{10\cdot 5} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.2$ | $0.6$ | $0.8$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.3$ | $0.7$ | $1$ |

The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=0.8\,\text{E}[Y]=0.7,\,\text{SD}[X]=0.4,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.4583,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 1\cdot 0.1 \\  & +1\cdot 0\cdot 0.2+1\cdot 1\cdot 0.6 \\  & =0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =0.6-(0.8)(0.7) \\  & =0.04.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{0.04}{0.4\cdot 0.4583} \\  & ≈0.22,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.

Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot (-4)\cdot 0.16+0\cdot 0\cdot 0.17+0\cdot 2\cdot 0.19 \\  & +10\cdot (-4)\cdot 0.15+10\cdot 0\cdot 0.17+10\cdot 2\cdot 0.16 \\  & =-2.8.\end{aligned}

| $X=4$ | $0.05$ | $0.05$ | $0.4$ | $0.5$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.45$ | $0.1$ | $0.45$ | $1$ |

The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=2,\,\text{E}[Y]=0,\,\text{SD}[X]=2,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈9.4868,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot (-10)\cdot 0.4+0\cdot 0\cdot 0.05+0\cdot 10\cdot 0.05 \\  & +4\cdot (-10)\cdot 0.05+4\cdot 0\cdot 0.05+4\cdot 10\cdot 0.4 \\  & =14.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =14-(2)(0) \\  & =14.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{14}{2\cdot 9.4868} \\  & ≈0.74,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 1\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 2\cdot 0.2 \\  & +1\cdot 0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 1\cdot 0.1+1\cdot 2\cdot 0.2 \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{-0.1}{0.4899\cdot 0.8944} \\  & ≈0.23,\end{aligned}

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{8}{5\pi },\,\text{E}[Y]=\frac{8}{5\pi },\,\text{SD}[X]≈0.2719,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.2719,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}xy\cdot \frac{8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}{\pi }\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }\text{ }{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}({x}^{3}y+x{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}[\frac{1}{4}{(1-{y}^{2})}^{2}y+\frac{1}{2}(1-{y}^{2}){y}^{3}]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}[(1-2{y}^{2}+{y}^{4})y+2(1-{y}^{2}){y}^{3}]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{2}{3\pi }-(\frac{8}{5\pi })(\frac{8}{5\pi }) \\  & =\frac{50\pi -192}{75{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(\frac{50\pi -192}{75{\pi }^{2}})}{(0.2719)\cdot (0.2719)} \\  & ≈-0.64,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{x+y}{3}, & \,0\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{11}{9},\,\text{E}[Y]=\frac{5}{9},\,\text{SD}[X]≈0.5329,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.2833,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot \frac{x+y}{3}\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x{y}^{3}}{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+\frac{x}{3})\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{6}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{6}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}-(\frac{11}{9})(\frac{5}{9}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{81}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(-\frac{1}{81})}{(0.5329)\cdot (0.2833)} \\  & ≈-0.08,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2}, & \,1\le x\le 2,\,0\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{4}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2,\,\text{E}[Y]=\frac{7}{12},\,\text{SD}[X]≈0.2898,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.2764,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}xy\cdot (\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{1}{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{2{y}^{2}}{x}+\frac{1}{2}xy)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[\frac{2}{3x}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}x{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(\frac{2}{3x}+\frac{1}{4}x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡x+\frac{1}{8}{x}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =(\frac{2}{3}\operatorname{ln}⁡2+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{8}) \\  & =\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}+\frac{3}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}+\frac{3}{8})-(\frac{3}{4}+\operatorname{ln}⁡2)(\frac{7}{12}) \\  & =(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{3}-\frac{7\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{12})+(\frac{3}{8}-\frac{7}{16}) \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{12}-\frac{1}{16}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡2}{12}-\frac{1}{16})}{(0.2898)\cdot (0.2764)} \\  & ≈-0.06,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}xy\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)}{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)]_{x=0}^{x=\pi /2}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[\frac{\pi }{2}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-y)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-y)-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(-y)]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{\pi }{2}y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)(y\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡y]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)\frac{\pi }{2}+1-(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)] \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}-4\pi +8}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}-4\pi +8}{8}-(\frac{\pi }{4})(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}-8\pi +16}{16} \\  & ={(\frac{\pi }{4}-1)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{{(\frac{\pi }{4}-1)}^{2}}{(0.4332)\cdot (0.4332)} \\  & ≈0.25,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem:
$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{9}{12}(xy+1), & \,{y}^{2}\le x\le 1,\,-1\le y\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{3}{5},\,\text{E}[Y]=\frac{1}{7},\,\text{SD}[X]≈0.2619,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.4238,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{1}xy\cdot \frac{9}{12}(xy+1)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+xy)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y]}_{x={y}^{2}}^{x=1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}y-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{8}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{[\frac{1}{9}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{27}{y}^{9}-\frac{1}{12}{y}^{6}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{9}{12}[\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{27}-\frac{1}{12}-(-\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{27}-\frac{1}{12})] \\  & =\frac{9}{12}(\frac{2}{9}-\frac{2}{27}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}-(\frac{3}{5})(\frac{1}{7}) \\  & =\frac{8}{315}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(\frac{8}{315})}{(0.2619)\cdot (0.4238)} \\  & ≈0.23,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Finding a Correlation Coefficient Given Variances and Covariance
canonical_examples.problem: The variances of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ are $25$ and $36,$ respectively. Given that $\textrm{Cov}[X,Y] = 18,$ find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{25}=5, \\ \text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[Y]}=\sqrt{36}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[X]} \\  & =\frac{18}{5\cdot 6} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$

\textrm {E}[Y]=0.6, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[X] \approx 0.4899, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[Y] \approx 0.4899,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 1\cdot 0.5 \\  & +1\cdot 0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 1\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =0.1-(0.4)(0.6) \\  & =-0.14.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{-0.14}{0.4899\cdot 0.4899} \\  & ≈-0.58,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\textrm {E}[X]= \dfrac{3}{4},\qquad
\textrm {E}[Y]= \dfrac{5}{12}, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[X]\approx 0.1936, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[Y]\approx 0.2444,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{x}xy\cdot 2(x+y)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{x}(2{x}^{2}y+2x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}x{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}+\frac{2}{3}{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{5}{3}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-(\frac{3}{4})(\frac{5}{12}) \\  & =\frac{1}{48}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(\frac{1}{48})}{(0.1936)\cdot (0.2444)} \\  & ≈0.44,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let $X$ and $Y$ be two random variables with covariance $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ and standard deviations $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y].$ 

The **correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y,$** also known as the **Pearson correlation coefficient**, is denoted $\rho$ (the Greek letter "rho") and is defined as

$$
\rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X]\cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]}.
$$

Note the following:

- The correlation coefficient satisfies

$$
-1\leq \rho \leq 1.
$$

- If $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables, then 

$$
\rho = 0.
$$

The reverse implication does not always hold. In other words, $\rho=0$ does *not* imply that $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

- Unlike the covariance, $\rho$ is a *dimensionless* quantity. This means we'll get the same answer regardless of the units used to measure $X$ and $Y.$

- Also unlike the covariance, $\rho$ tells the strength of the correlation between $X$ and $Y.$ We typically have the following rule of thumb:

- If $|\rho| \gt 0.7,$ the correlation is **strong,** and the data generated by our two random variables closely follow a straight line. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14227055/assets/3fd8b4e85bd76bbf78fdb2b135c49b3fd5e37fd9651dcae29d945d75aa45b905.png)

- If $0.3\leq |\rho| \leq 0.7,$ the correlation is **weak.** The data generated by our random variables follow a straight line, but many are far from the line.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14227055/assets/c132ec90770bb84ad6c7dcc4b24773a923139c616f523ba0a23c1506c40c508c.png)

- If $|\rho| \lt 0.3,$ then the correlation is **negligible.** No (linear) correlation exists between the data points generated by the random variables.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14227055/assets/9afa80bfadc40b8b832b17dcea10d66d5a08955909d5bea66c7c010558b5ea19.png)

Let's get some practice computing the correlation coefficient.

-1\leq \rho \leq 1.
$$

- If $X$ and $Y$ are independent random variables, then 

$$
\rho = 0.
$$

The reverse implication does not always hold. In other words, $\rho=0$ does *not* imply that $X$ and $Y$ are independent.

- Unlike the covariance, $\rho$ is a *dimensionless* quantity. This means we'll get the same answer regardless of the units used to measure $X$ and $Y.$

- Also unlike the covariance, $\rho$ tells the strength of the correlation between $X$ and $Y.$ We typically have the following rule of thumb:

- If $|\rho| \gt 0.7,$ the correlation is **strong,** and the data generated by our two random variables closely follow a straight line. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14227055/assets/3fd8b4e85bd76bbf78fdb2b135c49b3fd5e37fd9651dcae29d945d75aa45b905.png)

- If $0.3\leq |\rho| \leq 0.7,$ the correlation is **weak.** The data generated by our random variables follow a straight line, but many are far from the line.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14227055/assets/c132ec90770bb84ad6c7dcc4b24773a923139c616f523ba0a23c1506c40c508c.png)

- If $|\rho| \lt 0.3,$ then the correlation is **negligible.** No (linear) correlation exists between the data points generated by the random variables.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/differential/14227055/assets/9afa80bfadc40b8b832b17dcea10d66d5a08955909d5bea66c7c010558b5ea19.png)

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{25}=5, \\ \text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[Y]}=\sqrt{36}=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[X]} \\  & =\frac{18}{5\cdot 6} \\  & =\frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.name: Example: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Discrete Random Variables
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Correlation Coefficient Given Variances and Covariance
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 1\cdot 0.5 \\  & +1\cdot 0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 1\cdot 0.1 \\  & =0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =0.1-(0.4)(0.6) \\  & =-0.14.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{-0.14}{0.4899\cdot 0.4899} \\  & ≈-0.58,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

The joint probability mass function f(x,y) for the discrete random variables X and Y is shown above. Given that E[X]=2,E[Y]=0,SD[X]=2,SD[Y]≈9.4868, find the correlation coefficient of X and Y. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

a
0.56
b
−0.84
c
0.74
d
0.63
e
−0.35
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables X and Y is defined as

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y],

where

  • Cov[X,Y] is the covariance, and

  • SD[X] and SD[Y] are the standard deviations of X and Y.

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

E[XY]=∑x∈SX∑y∈SYxyf(x,y)=0⋅(−10)⋅0.4+0⋅0⋅0.05+0⋅10⋅0.05=+4⋅(−10)⋅0.05+4⋅0⋅0.05+4⋅10⋅0.4=14.

Then, we compute the covariance and get

Cov[X,Y]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y]=14−(2)(0)=14.

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y]≈142⋅9.4868≈0.74,

rounded to 2 decimal places.
question.knowledge_point: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Discrete Random Variables

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Discrete Random Variables
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 1\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 2\cdot 0.2 \\  & +1\cdot 0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 1\cdot 0.1+1\cdot 2\cdot 0.2 \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =0.5-(0.6)(1) \\  & =-0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{-0.1}{0.4899\cdot 0.8944} \\  & ≈0.23,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Discrete Random Variables

observed_steps.name: Example: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Continuous Random Variables
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Discrete Random Variables
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{x}xy\cdot 2(x+y)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{x}(2{x}^{2}y+2x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}x{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}+\frac{2}{3}{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{5}{3}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-(\frac{3}{4})(\frac{5}{12}) \\  & =\frac{1}{48}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\textrm {E}[X]= \dfrac{3}{4},\qquad
\textrm {E}[Y]= \dfrac{5}{12}, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[X]\approx 0.1936, \qquad
\textrm {SD}[Y]\approx 0.2444,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho = \dfrac{\textrm{Cov}[X, Y] }{\textrm {SD}[X] \cdot \textrm {SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\textrm{Cov}[X, Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\textrm {SD}[X]$ and $\textrm {SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{x}xy\cdot 2(x+y)\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{x}(2{x}^{2}y+2x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y]\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}x{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=x}\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{4}+\frac{2}{3}{x}^{4})\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{5}{3}{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{5}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{3}-(\frac{3}{4})(\frac{5}{12}) \\  & =\frac{1}{48}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(\frac{1}{48})}{(0.1936)\cdot (0.2444)} \\  & ≈0.44,\end{aligned}

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Continuous Random Variables
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician and integration by parts, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}xy\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)}{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}xy\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[xy\operatorname{sin}⁡(x-y)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-y)]_{x=0}^{x=\pi /2}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}[\frac{\pi }{2}y\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-y)+y\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}-y)-y\operatorname{cos}⁡(-y)]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\frac{\pi }{2}y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+y\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)(y\operatorname{sin}⁡y+\operatorname{cos}⁡y)+\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡y]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}[(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)\frac{\pi }{2}+1-(\frac{\pi }{2}-1)] \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}-4\pi +8}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}-4\pi +8}{8}-(\frac{\pi }{4})(\frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =\frac{{\pi }^{2}-8\pi +16}{16} \\  & ={(\frac{\pi }{4}-1)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{{(\frac{\pi }{4}-1)}^{2}}{(0.4332)\cdot (0.4332)} \\  & ≈0.25,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{1}xy\cdot \frac{9}{12}(xy+1)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}[{\int }_{{y}^{2}}^{1}({x}^{2}{y}^{2}+xy)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}y]}_{x={y}^{2}}^{x=1}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}y-\frac{1}{3}{y}^{8}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{9}{12}{[\frac{1}{9}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{4}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{27}{y}^{9}-\frac{1}{12}{y}^{6}]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =\frac{9}{12}[\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{27}-\frac{1}{12}-(-\frac{1}{9}+\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{27}-\frac{1}{12})] \\  & =\frac{9}{12}(\frac{2}{9}-\frac{2}{27}) \\  & =\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{1}{9}-(\frac{3}{5})(\frac{1}{7}) \\  & =\frac{8}{315}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(\frac{8}{315})}{(0.2619)\cdot (0.4238)} \\  & ≈0.23,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

Question 15

f(x,y)={912(xy+1),y2≤x≤1,−1≤y≤10,otherwise

The joint probability density function f(x,y) for the continuous random variables X and Y is shown above. Given that E[X]=35,E[Y]=17,SD[X]≈0.2619,SD[Y]≈0.4238, find the correlation coefficient of X and Y. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

a
0.23
b
0.12
c
−0.03
d
−0.11
e
0.08
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables X and Y is defined as

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y],

where

  • Cov[X,Y] is the covariance, and

  • SD[X] and SD[Y] are the standard deviations of X and Y.

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

E[XY]=∬R2xyf(x,y)dxdy=∫−11[∫y21xy⋅912(xy+1)dx]dy=912∫−11[∫y21(x2y2+xy)dx]dy=912∫−11[13x3y2+12x2y]x=y2x=1dy=912∫−11(13y2+12y−13y8−12y5)dy=912[19y3+14y2−127y9−112y6]−11=912[19+14−127−112−(−19+14+127−112)]=912(29−227)=19.

Then, we compute the covariance and get

Cov[X,Y]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y]=19−(35)(17)=8315.

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y]≈(8315)(0.2619)⋅(0.4238)≈0.23,

rounded to 2 decimal places.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Correlation Coefficient Given Variances and Covariance
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & =\frac{-3}{3\cdot 2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Given that Cov[X,Y]=−3, SD[X]=3, and SD[Y]=2, find the correlation coefficient of the random variables X and Y.

a
 −13
b
 −12
c
 −32
d
 12
e
 36
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables X and Y is defined as

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y],

where

  • Cov[X,Y] is the covariance, and

  • SD[X] and SD[Y] are the standard deviations of X and Y.

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y]=−33⋅2=−12.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Given that $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=-9,$ $\text{SD}[X]=2,$ and $\text{SD}[Y]=5$, find the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Given that $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=5,$ $\text{SD}[X]=2,$ and $\text{SD}[Y]=4$, find the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & =\frac{5}{2\cdot 4} \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem: Given that $\text{Cov}[X,Y]=5,$ $\text{SD}[X]=2,$ and $\text{SD}[Y]=4$, find the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y.$
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & =\frac{5}{2\cdot 4} \\  & =\frac{5}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: The variances of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ are $0.09$ and $0.16$, respectively. Given that $\text{Cov}(X,Y)=-0.03,$ find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[X]}=\sqrt{0.09}=0.3, \\ \text{SD}[X] & =\sqrt{\text{Var}[Y]}=\sqrt{0.16}=0.4.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[X]} \\  & =\frac{-0.03}{0.3\cdot 0.4} \\  & =-0.25.\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding a Correlation Coefficient Given Variances and Covariance
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & =\frac{15}{10\cdot 5} \\  & =\frac{3}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Given that Cov[X,Y]=15, SD[X]=10, and SD[Y]=5, find the correlation coefficient of the random variables X and Y.

a
310
b
310
c
61000
d
3100
e
310
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables X and Y is defined as

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y],

where

  • Cov[X,Y] is the covariance, and

  • SD[X] and SD[Y] are the standard deviations of X and Y.

Substituting our data in the formula, we obtain

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y]=1510⋅5=310.

question.problem:
| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.2$ | $0.6$ | $0.8$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.3$ | $0.7$ | $1$ |

The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=0.8\,\text{E}[Y]=0.7,\,\text{SD}[X]=0.4,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.4583,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 1\cdot 0.1 \\  & +1\cdot 0\cdot 0.2+1\cdot 1\cdot 0.6 \\  & =0.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =0.6-(0.8)(0.7) \\  & =0.04.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{0.04}{0.4\cdot 0.4583} \\  & ≈0.22,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

The joint probability mass function f(x,y) for the discrete random variables X and Y is shown above. Given that E[X]=0.8E[Y]=0.7,SD[X]=0.4,SD[Y]≈0.4583, find the correlation coefficient of X and Y. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

a
0.56
b
−0.35
c
0.22
d
0.16
e
−0.32
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables X and Y is defined as

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y],

where

  • Cov[X,Y] is the covariance, and

  • SD[X] and SD[Y] are the standard deviations of X and Y.

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

E[XY]=∑x∈SX∑y∈SYxyf(x,y)=0⋅0⋅0.1+0⋅1⋅0.1=+1⋅0⋅0.2+1⋅1⋅0.6=0.6.

Then, we compute the covariance and get

Cov[X,Y]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y]=0.6−(0.8)(0.7)=0.04.

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y]≈0.040.4⋅0.4583≈0.22,

rounded to 2 decimal places.

question.name: Question 7
question.problem:
| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=-4$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.16$ | $0.17$ | $0.19$ | $0.52$ |
| $X=10$ | $0.15$ | $0.17$ | $0.16$ | $0.48$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.31$ | $0.34$ | $0.35$ | $1$ |

The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=4.8,\,\text{E}[Y]=-0.54,\,\text{SD}[X]≈4.9960,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈2.4634,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot (-4)\cdot 0.16+0\cdot 0\cdot 0.17+0\cdot 2\cdot 0.19 \\  & +10\cdot (-4)\cdot 0.15+10\cdot 0\cdot 0.17+10\cdot 2\cdot 0.16 \\  & =-2.8.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =-2.8-(4.8)(-0.54) \\  & =-0.208.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{-0.208}{4.9960\cdot 2.4634} \\  & ≈-0.02,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.html:
Question 8
?
f(x,y) Y=−10 Y=0 Y=10 fX
X=0 0.4 0.05 0.05 0.5
X=4 0.05 0.05 0.4 0.5
fY 0.45 0.1 0.45 1

The joint probability mass function f(x,y) for the discrete random variables X and Y is shown above. Given that E[X]=2,E[Y]=0,SD[X]=2,SD[Y]≈9.4868, find the correlation coefficient of X and Y. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

a
0.56
b
−0.84
c
0.74
d
0.63
e
−0.35
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables X and Y is defined as

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y],

where

  • Cov[X,Y] is the covariance, and

  • SD[X] and SD[Y] are the standard deviations of X and Y.

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

E[XY]=∑x∈SX∑y∈SYxyf(x,y)=0⋅(−10)⋅0.4+0⋅0⋅0.05+0⋅10⋅0.05=+4⋅(−10)⋅0.05+4⋅0⋅0.05+4⋅10⋅0.4=14.

Then, we compute the covariance and get

Cov[X,Y]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y]=14−(2)(0)=14.

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y]≈142⋅9.4868≈0.74,

rounded to 2 decimal places.

solution.reasoning: E[XY]=4(-10)(0.05)+4(10)(0.4)=14. Thus Cov[X,Y]=14-(2)(0)=14, and the correlation is 14/(2·9.4868)≈0.7379, rounding to 0.74, option c. No Math Academy answer key or grade for this question is captured; the worked example concerns a different question.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.problem:
| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=-10$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=10$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.4$ | $0.05$ | $0.05$ | $0.5$ |
| $X=4$ | $0.05$ | $0.05$ | $0.4$ | $0.5$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.45$ | $0.1$ | $0.45$ | $1$ |

The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=2,\,\text{E}[Y]=0,\,\text{SD}[X]=2,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈9.4868,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
feedback.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot (-10)\cdot 0.4+0\cdot 0\cdot 0.05+0\cdot 10\cdot 0.05 \\  & +4\cdot (-10)\cdot 0.05+4\cdot 0\cdot 0.05+4\cdot 10\cdot 0.4 \\  & =14.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =14-(2)(0) \\  & =14.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{14}{2\cdot 9.4868} \\  & ≈0.74,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

question.name: Question 9
question.problem:
| $f(x,y)$ | $Y=0$ | $Y=1$ | $Y=2$ | ${f}_{X}$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $X=0$ | $0.1$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.4$ |
| $X=1$ | $0.3$ | $0.1$ | $0.2$ | $0.6$ |
| ${f}_{Y}$ | $0.4$ | $0.2$ | $0.4$ | $1$ |

The joint probability mass function $f(x,y)$ for the discrete random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=0.6,\,\text{E}[Y]=1,\,\text{SD}[X]≈0.4899,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.8944,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot 0\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 1\cdot 0.1+0\cdot 2\cdot 0.2 \\  & +1\cdot 0\cdot 0.3+1\cdot 1\cdot 0.1+1\cdot 2\cdot 0.2 \\  & =0.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =0.5-(0.6)(1) \\  & =-0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{-0.1}{0.4899\cdot 0.8944} \\  & ≈0.23,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

last_observation.name: Question 10
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Finding the Correlation Coefficient of Two Discrete Random Variables
last_observation.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={\sum }_{x\in {S}_{X}}{\sum }_{y\in {S}_{Y}}xy\,f(x,y) \\  & =0\cdot (-1)\cdot 0.2+0\cdot 1\cdot 0.5 \\  & +1\cdot (-1)\cdot 0.2+1\cdot 1\cdot 0.1 \\  & =-0.1.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =-0.1-(0.3)(0.2) \\  & =-0.16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{-0.16}{0.4583\cdot 0.9798} \\  & ≈-0.36,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $2$ decimal places.

Question 10
?
f(x,y) Y=−1 Y=1 fX
X=0 0.2 0.5 0.7
X=1 0.2 0.1 0.3
fY 0.4 0.6 1

The joint probability mass function f(x,y) for the discrete random variables X and Y is shown above. Given that E[X]=0.3E[Y]=0.2,SD[X]≈0.4583,SD[Y]≈0.9798, find the correlation coefficient of X and Y. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

a
−0.60
b
−0.36
c
0.16
d
−0.22
e
0.32
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the correlation coefficient of random variables X and Y is defined as

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y],

where

  • Cov[X,Y] is the covariance, and

  • SD[X] and SD[Y] are the standard deviations of X and Y.

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

E[XY]=∑x∈SX∑y∈SYxyf(x,y)=0⋅(−1)⋅0.2+0⋅1⋅0.5=+1⋅(−1)⋅0.2+1⋅1⋅0.1=−0.1.

Then, we compute the covariance and get

Cov[X,Y]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y]=−0.1−(0.3)(0.2)=−0.16.

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y]≈−0.160.4583⋅0.9798≈−0.36,

rounded to 2 decimal places.

question.name: Question 11
question.problem:
$$
f(x,y)=\{\begin{aligned}\frac{8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}{\pi }, & \,x\ge 0,\,y\ge 0,\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\le 1 \\ 0, & \,\text{otherwise}\end{aligned}
$$

The joint probability density function $f(x,y)$ for the continuous random variables $X$ and $Y$ is shown above. Given that 

$$
\text{E}[X]=\frac{8}{5\pi },\,\text{E}[Y]=\frac{8}{5\pi },\,\text{SD}[X]≈0.2719,\,\text{SD}[Y]≈0.2719,
$$

 
find the correlation coefficient of $X$ and $Y.$ Round your answer to $2$ decimal places.
question.worked_solution:
Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables $X$ and $Y$ is defined as

$$
\rho =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]},
$$

where

- $\text{Cov}[X,Y]$ is the covariance, and

- $\text{SD}[X]$ and $\text{SD}[Y]$ are the standard deviations of $X$ and $Y.$

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[XY] & ={∬}_{{R}^{2}}xy\,f(x,y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}xy\cdot \frac{8({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})}{\pi }\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }\text{ }{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}({x}^{3}y+x{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x]\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{4}{x}^{4}y+\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}]}_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{1-{y}^{2}}}\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{8}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}[\frac{1}{4}{(1-{y}^{2})}^{2}y+\frac{1}{2}(1-{y}^{2}){y}^{3}]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}[(1-2{y}^{2}+{y}^{4})y+2(1-{y}^{2}){y}^{3}]\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}(y-{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }{[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}-\frac{1}{6}{y}^{6}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{3\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we compute the covariance and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Cov}[X,Y] & =\text{E}[XY]-\text{E}[X]\cdot \text{E}[Y] \\  & =\frac{2}{3\pi }-(\frac{8}{5\pi })(\frac{8}{5\pi }) \\  & =\frac{50\pi -192}{75{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is 

$$
\begin{aligned}\rho  & =\frac{\text{Cov}[X,Y]}{\text{SD}[X]\cdot \text{SD}[Y]} \\  & ≈\frac{(\frac{50\pi -192}{75{\pi }^{2}})}{(0.2719)\cdot (0.2719)} \\  & ≈-0.64,\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11

f(x,y)={8(x2+y2)π,x≥0,y≥0,x2+y2≤10,otherwise

The joint probability density function f(x,y) for the continuous random variables X and Y is shown above. Given that E[X]=85π,E[Y]=85π,SD[X]≈0.2719,SD[Y]≈0.2719, find the correlation coefficient of X and Y. Round your answer to 2 decimal places.

a
−0.64
b
0.35
c
−0.75
d
0.27
e
−0.47
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Recall that the correlation coefficient of the random variables X and Y is defined as

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y],

where

  • Cov[X,Y] is the covariance, and

  • SD[X] and SD[Y] are the standard deviations of X and Y.

First, by applying the rule of the lazy statistician, we have

E[XY]=∬R2xyf(x,y)dxdy=∫01[∫01−y2xy⋅8(x2+y2)πdx]dy=8π ∫01[∫01−y2(x3y+xy3)dx]dy=8π∫01[14x4y+12x2y3]x=0x=1−y2dy=8π∫01[14(1−y2)2y+12(1−y2)y3]dy=2π∫01[(1−2y2+y4)y+2(1−y2)y3]dy=2π∫01(y−y5)dy=2π[12y2−16y6]01=23π

Then, we compute the covariance and get

Cov[X,Y]=E[XY]−E[X]⋅E[Y]=23π−(85π)(85π)=50π−19275π2.

Therefore, the correlation coefficient is

ρ=Cov[X,Y]SD[X]⋅SD[Y]≈(50π−19275π2)(0.2719)⋅(0.2719)≈−0.64,

rounded to 2 decimal places.
