question.name: Question 7
question.problem: $\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x-4x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x+4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)-\frac{1}{26}\operatorname{sin}⁡(13x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

question.html:
Question 7
?

∫sin⁡(9x)sin⁡(4x)dx=

a
110sin⁡(13x)−126sin⁡(5x)+C
b
110sin⁡(5x)−126sin⁡(13x)+C
c
110cos⁡(5x)−126cos⁡(13x)+C
d
110sin⁡(5x)+126sin⁡(13x)+C
e
15sin⁡(5x)−113sin⁡(13x)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine: cos⁡(α−β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β+sin⁡αsin⁡βcos⁡(α+β)=cos⁡αcos⁡β−sin⁡αsin⁡β

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity: cos⁡(α−β)−cos⁡(α+β)=2sin⁡αsin⁡βsin⁡αsin⁡β=12(cos⁡(α−β)−cos⁡(α+β))

Thus, we have sin⁡(9x)sin⁡(4x)=12(cos⁡(9x−4x)−cos⁡(9x+4x))=12(cos⁡(5x)−cos⁡(13x)).

Substituting this into the integral gives ∫sin⁡(9x)sin⁡(4x)dx=∫12cos⁡(5x)−12cos⁡(13x)dx=110sin⁡(5x)−126sin⁡(13x)+C, where C is an arbitrary constant.

last_observation.name: Question 7
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Integrating a Product of Sines
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x-4x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x+4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)-\frac{1}{26}\operatorname{sin}⁡(13x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem: $\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x=$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x-4x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x+4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(13x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)-\frac{1}{26}\operatorname{sin}⁡(13x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

question.name: Question 8
question.problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for cosine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Subtracting the second equation from the first, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha -\beta )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\alpha +\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(x-4x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(-3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(5x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)-\frac{1}{10}\operatorname{sin}⁡(5x)]}_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{10}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{15\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{1}{6}(1-0)-\frac{1}{10}(-1-0) \\  & =\frac{4}{15}.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x+6x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x-6x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(-3x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(9x)-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(3x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{cos}⁡(9x)+\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{cos}⁡(3x)]}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))+\frac{1}{6}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}(0-1)+\frac{1}{6}(0-1) \\  & =-\frac{1}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x+4x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x-4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{28}\operatorname{cos}⁡(14x)-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

Question 13
?

∫sin⁡(10x)cos⁡(4x)dx=

a
128sin⁡(14x)+124sin⁡(6x)+C
b
−114sin⁡(14x)−16sin⁡(6x)+C
c
−128cos⁡(10x)+112sin⁡(4x)+C
d
−120cos⁡(10x)+18sin⁡(4x)+C
e
−128cos⁡(14x)−112cos⁡(6x)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine: sin⁡(α+β)=sin⁡αcos⁡β+cos⁡αsin⁡βsin⁡(α−β)=sin⁡αcos⁡β−cos⁡αsin⁡β

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity: sin⁡(α+β)+sin⁡(α−β)=2sin⁡αcos⁡βsin⁡αcos⁡β=12(sin⁡(α+β)+sin⁡(α−β))

Thus, we have sin⁡(10x)cos⁡(4x)=12(sin⁡(10x+4x)+sin⁡(10x−4x))=12(sin⁡(14x)+sin⁡(6x)).

Substituting this into the integral gives ∫sin⁡(10x)cos⁡(4x)dx=∫12sin⁡(14x)+12sin⁡(6x)dx=−128cos⁡(14x)−112cos⁡(6x)+C, where C is an arbitrary constant.

last_observation.name: Question 13
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Integrating a Product of Sine and Cosine
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x+4x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x-4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{28}\operatorname{cos}⁡(14x)-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.problem: $\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x=$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x+4x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(10x-4x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(10x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x)\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(14x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{1}{28}\operatorname{cos}⁡(14x)-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C$ is an arbitrary constant.

question.name: Question 14
question.problem:
Evaluate the following integral.

${\int }_{0}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=$ {{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
First, let's recall the sum and difference formulas for sine:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta +\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta -\operatorname{cos}⁡\alpha \operatorname{sin}⁡\beta \end{aligned}
$$

Adding these equations, we get the following product-to-sum identity:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ) & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  \\ \operatorname{sin}⁡\alpha \operatorname{cos}⁡\beta  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha +\beta )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\alpha -\beta ))\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x) & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x+x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x-x)) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting this into the integral gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /4}\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8x)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(6x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{16}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8x)-\frac{1}{12}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6x)]}_{0}^{3\pi /4} \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0))-\frac{1}{12}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{9\pi }{2})-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)) \\  & =-\frac{1}{16}(1-1)-\frac{1}{12}(0-1) \\  & =\frac{1}{12}.\end{aligned}
$$
